passages.where: At the start of his search the Teacher says all things are wearisome, more than one can describe: the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear content with hearing. The site's note on the chapter says he set out to explore everything done under heaven and found wisdom itself a source of grief. The appetite for more to see and hear is old, and it has never been satisfied by more.

The book's closing voice praises the Teacher's careful work and then warns that there is no end to the making of many books, and much study wearies the body. The site's note says this frame narrator gives the conclusion: fear God and keep his commandments. More words are not the same as wisdom, and the book ends by pointing past all of them to God.

A father urges his son to guard his heart with all diligence, for from it flow the springs of life, and, as the site's note says, to guard his speech, his eyes and his steps as well. The site's note on the chapter explains that in Hebrew thought the heart is the place of thinking, deciding, remembering and desiring. What a person lets in shapes all of that.

In the parable of the sower, the seed among thorns is heard, but the worries of this life, the deceitfulness of wealth and the desire for other things come in and choke it. The site's note says none of the three is described as scandalous sin; all are ordinary. The plain note asks whether a life has become too full to give the word room.

The first psalm blesses the person who does not take the counsel of the wicked or sit with mockers, but whose delight is in the law of the LORD, meditating on it day and night. The site's plain note asks where drifting has become sitting, and suggests reading a few lines of Scripture slowly and returning to them during the day. To meditate is to let a few words go deep, the opposite of taking in many quickly.

Writing about food offered to idols, Paul agrees with the Corinthians' knowledge and then says knowledge puffs up, but love builds up. The site's note says knowledge without love can destroy a fellow believer, and the plain note asks when being right has mattered more than the person in front of us. Knowing more about everything does not make anyone more loving.

Luke remarks that the Athenians and foreigners in the city spent their time doing nothing but hearing and talking about new ideas. The site's plain note says Paul, troubled by what the city worshipped, went to talk with people rather than away from them. A life spent on the newest thing can leave no room for the one thing that matters.

At Horeb the LORD passes by, and he is not in the great wind, the earthquake or the fire, but in a still, small voice. The site's note on the chapter tells how God then answered Elijah's complaint with new work. God is often not found in the loudest thing, and a mind full of noise can miss what is quiet.

When Judah's leaders sent envoys and treasure to Egypt without asking God, he told them their strength would lie in repentance, rest and quiet confidence, but they were not willing. The site's note says he still longs to be gracious and will answer their cry. Quiet in Scripture is not idleness; it is trust that does not need to rush toward every source of help.

Paul prays that the Philippians' love will abound in knowledge and depth of insight, so that they may test and approve what is best. The site's plain note asks the reader to pray this for someone they love: not only that their troubles end, but that their love grows wiser. The aim of knowing is discernment and love, not more knowing.

misread.taken: The eye is the lamp of the body is often quoted as if it were only a rule about what to watch, a verse for screens and nothing else.
misread.says: The site's note says that in context the saying stands between Jesus' words on treasure and on masters, and concerns how a person looks at money: the generous eye fills life with light, the grasping eye darkens it. The same note sets out an ancient picture of the eye as a lamp shining from the body's inner light. Applying it to what we watch is not wrong, but the verse asks first what the heart is fixed on, and greed can darken a life as surely as anything on a screen.

whole: Many people end the day having read a hundred headlines, a dozen arguments, several crises and countless opinions, and feel more tired and less sure of anything than when they began. The phone is checked before the eyes are fully open and again in the last minutes before sleep. Attention slips from one thing to the next, and it becomes hard to read a long page, sit through a conversation, or pray for more than a minute. It feels like being informed. Often it is closer to being flooded: knowing a little about everything, and having no time left to know anything, or anyone, well.

Scripture saw the hunger underneath long before the feeds. The eye is not satisfied with seeing, the Teacher says, nor the ear with hearing, and there is no end to the making of many books. The Athenians spent their time on nothing but new ideas. Paul warned that knowledge puffs up while love builds up. The Bible does not despise learning; it praises the discerning heart that seeks knowledge. But it knows that more information does not make a person wiser, and that what we take in shapes the heart, the place of thinking, deciding and desiring. Some of our overload is fear of missing something, some is restlessness, some is a way to avoid silence, and all of us have reached for the phone to avoid sitting with a thought, a person or God.

So the Bible's wisdom is to guard the heart and to choose what goes into it. Meditate on a few true words rather than skimming many, as Psalm 1 says. Keep times and places without the flood: the first minutes of the morning, the table, the last hour before sleep, one day in seven. Notice what leaves you more loving and what leaves you puffed up, anxious or numb, and take less of the second. Read something long and slow. Listen for the still, small voice, which is easy to miss when everything else is loud. And pray, as Paul did, for love that grows in knowledge and insight, so that you can tell what is best rather than only what is new.

The hope Scripture gives is that you do not need to know everything, because God does. His strength for his people lay in quiet confidence, not in rushing toward every source of help. The conclusion of the book that warns about many books is short: fear God and keep his commandments. A life rooted near the water, the first psalm says, bears fruit in season. There is more to hear than any person can take in, and you are free not to try.
sit: What do you reach for when there is a quiet moment, and what might you hear if you let one of those moments stay quiet?

prayer.lead: A short song of a soul that has stopped reaching for things too great for it. The site's plain note says it does not say those things do not matter; it says you can be quiet with God while they wait.
